name: NestAway
epitaph: Found homes for thousands. Couldn't keep its own.
oneLiner: A rental app that ran landlords’ flats as furnished homes for young professionals, handling rent, moving and repairs for a cut.
causeOfDeath: It spent ₹3–4 for every ₹1 earned, failed to raise its big round in 2019, and Covid emptied its homes. It sold at a 95% discount.
moneyNote: TechCrunch reports $115M raised and a $227M valuation in 2019 (Entrackr says $110M and $220M). Sale price: up to ₹90 crore in cash, about $11M at 2023 rates (~₹82 per dollar). Rupee figures are from filings.
inOneMinute: NestAway turned landlords' empty flats into **ready-to-move homes for young professionals** and took a cut of every month's rent.
It never made the model pay. In FY18 it **lost ₹157 crore on ₹47 crore of revenue**; staff costs alone were double its revenue.
Its big 2019 round stalled, then Covid hit. Listings fell from 50,000 to 18,000, and it **sold for about $11 million**.
killerLine: A small cut of a cheap product needs a tiny cost base. **If every rupee earned costs ₹3 to deliver, scale only makes the hole deeper.**

chapters.title: The idea: renting without the headache
chapters.body: Moving to a new city in India for your first job is hard. Landlords often don't want bachelors, brokers charge a month's rent, and deposits can be huge. NestAway, founded in 2015, offered a fix. It **took landlords' flats, furnished them, and rented them room by room** to young professionals. Tenants paid rent, asked for repairs and moved in through an app. NestAway earned a percentage of each home's monthly rent. By April 2016 it said it had found homes for 10,000 tenants in Bengaluru, Delhi, Pune and Hyderabad, and raised **$30 million led by Tiger Global**. Tiger's Lee Fixel called it an "annuity-based e-commerce model at scale". It solved a real and painful problem.

chapters.title: The rise: big costs, small cut
chapters.body: The trouble was the maths. NestAway earned only a slice of rent, but it had to find homes, furnish them, find tenants, collect rent and fix leaking taps. That needs lots of people. In FY18 its revenue was ₹47 crore. Its **staff costs alone were ₹93.5 crore**, double the revenue. Its loss rose to ₹156.8 crore, and it spent ₹4.30 for every ₹1 it earned. At the same time, it had **₹294 crore parked in mutual funds**, money raised from investors and waiting to be spent. Goldman Sachs invested in 2018. In 2019 NestAway set out to raise a huge Series D of $100–150 million, at a valuation reported at around $220–227 million.

chapters.title: The cracks: new brands, missing money
chapters.body: The big round never fully arrived. By September 2019 only about **$20 million had come in**, in small pieces from Tiger Global, Chiratae, Ratan Tata's UC-RNT fund and Goldman Sachs. Instead of fixing the core, NestAway spread out. In 2019 it launched **Hello World**, a co-living and co-working brand, set up a company for senior living, and planned a women's housing platform. Entrackr reported that the founders had slowed fundraising to focus on these new entities. Co-founder Deepak Dhar left in July 2019, and more than four senior vice-presidents left within months. Revenue did rise to ₹108.9 crore in FY20. Then the pandemic arrived, and young professionals left cities for their hometowns.

chapters.title: The fall: Covid and a fire sale
chapters.body: With offices shut, tenants moved out and rooms sat empty. Properties on NestAway fell from **about 50,000 before Covid to 18,000**. Revenue fell to ₹90.7 crore in FY21 and ₹57.9 crore in FY22, while the loss grew to ₹95 crore. In FY22 it spent ₹3.08 for every ₹1 of revenue. In June 2022 Aurum PropTech bought the Hello World co-living unit. A year later, in June 2023, Aurum agreed to buy NestAway itself for **up to ₹90 crore, about $11 million**, a 95% cut from its 2019 valuation. TechCrunch called it "a near complete erosion in value" for investors who had put in over $100 million.

charts.title: Revenue vs loss
charts.takeaway: In every year with published numbers, NestAway's loss was bigger than or close to its revenue.

mistakes.title: A people-heavy business living on a small cut
mistakes.explain: NestAway earned a percentage of rent but did the work of a property manager, broker and repair service. In FY18 **staff costs were ₹93.5 crore on revenue of ₹47 crore**. It spent ₹4.30 for each ₹1 earned. When your share of each sale is small, your cost of serving each customer must be smaller.

mistakes.title: New brands before the core worked
mistakes.explain: In 2019, while losses were large and the Series D was stuck, NestAway launched co-living brand Hello World, a senior-living company and plans for women's housing. Entrackr reported the founders **slowed fundraising to focus on the new entities**. More businesses meant more cost and less attention on the one that paid the bills.

mistakes.title: Betting on a giant round that never came
mistakes.explain: The plan needed $100–150 million. By September 2019, **only about $20 million had arrived**. A company built for a big round has to cut fast if the round stalls. Instead, the pandemic arrived first, with costs still high. Hope is not a funding plan.

mistakes.title: No cushion for a shock
mistakes.explain: Its model depended on young workers living in cities. Covid sent them home, and listings fell from **about 50,000 to 18,000**. Any business that serves one group of customers in one situation should ask what happens if that situation disappears overnight.

warningSigns: Are our staff costs bigger than our revenue?
Do we earn only a small cut of each transaction but do most of the work ourselves?
Are we launching new brands or products while our first one still loses money on each customer?
Does our plan depend on a funding round that is less than half closed?
Would a single event (a lockdown, a law, a big rival) remove most of our customers at once?
Have several senior leaders left within the same few months?

lessons.title: Price for the work you actually do
lessons.detail: If you handle repairs, moving and rent collection, a small commission may not cover it. Work out the full cost of serving one customer for a year, then make sure your fee is bigger.

lessons.title: Automate or cut before you hire
lessons.detail: NestAway's costs were mostly people. Before adding staff to grow, ask which tasks software, partners or customers themselves could do.

lessons.title: One business at a time
lessons.detail: Launching new brands feels like progress, but each one splits your money and focus. Make the first business profitable per customer before starting the second.

lessons.title: Have a Plan B for the round
lessons.detail: When you go out to raise, also write the plan for raising only 20% of the target. Know in advance which costs you will cut, and cut them on the day you know.

lessons.title: Stress-test your customer
lessons.detail: Ask: what if our main customers suddenly can't or won't use us for six months? If the answer is 'we die', build a cash buffer or a second customer group.

quote.text: NestAway's customized strategy has demonstrated the potential to transform India's rental housing market.
quote.who: Lee Fixel, partner at Tiger Global
quote.context: On leading NestAway's $30 million Series C in April 2016, seven years before it sold for about $11 million.

afterlife.text: Aurum PropTech, which had already bought Hello World, took over NestAway in 2023 and said it would invest about $3.6 million to stabilise it. In January 2025 co-founder Amarendra Sahu filed a police complaint (FIR) alleging cheating and forgery in the sale against investors Tiger Global, Goldman Sachs and Chiratae and two co-founders. Co-founder Jitendra Jagadev said similar claims had been dismissed by the NCLT and called it harassment. No court had ruled on the FIR in the sources we read.
